title: Google Cloud Professional Machine Learning Engineer

nodes.title: Google Vertex AI (PDE / PCA): Key Ideas
nodes.content: Vertex AI is GCP's unified ML platform — it replaces AI Platform, AutoML, and several standalone services under one API surface. PDE and PCA exams test Feature Store for feature reuse, Model Registry for versioning, Pipelines for reproducibility, and the trade-offs between AutoML and custom training.

flashcards.front: AutoML vs custom training on Vertex AI — when do you choose each?
flashcards.back: AutoML: no ML code required — provide labeled data, Vertex trains and optimizes a model for you. Best for teams without ML expertise or for tabular/vision/NLP tasks where a proven architecture suffices. Custom training: bring your own code (TensorFlow, PyTorch, scikit-learn) in a custom container — required when you need a specific architecture, preprocessing logic, or domain-specific objectives that AutoML doesn't expose.

flashcards.front: Vertex AI Feature Store — what problem does it solve?
flashcards.back: Feature Store is a centralized, managed repository for ML features. It solves training–serving skew (the exact same feature computation is used for both offline training and online inference), enables feature reuse across teams and models, and provides point-in-time correct lookups to avoid data leakage. Features are stored as entity–feature–timestamp tuples and can be served online (low-latency) or offline (batch).

flashcards.front: Vertex AI Model Registry vs Endpoint — what is each?
flashcards.back: Model Registry: versioned catalog of trained model artifacts — stores metadata, lineage, and performance metrics. Uploading a model here doesn't serve it. Endpoint: a deployed, load-balanced serving resource that routes prediction requests to one or more model versions. You import a model from the Registry into an Endpoint to serve traffic; a single endpoint can hold multiple model versions with traffic splits for A/B testing.

flashcards.front: Online prediction vs batch prediction — pick the right one.
flashcards.back: Online prediction: real-time, low-latency (< 200 ms) REST calls against a deployed Endpoint — use when a user or application needs an immediate answer. Batch prediction: Vertex reads a BigQuery table or GCS file, runs inference on all rows, writes results back — use for scheduled scoring of large datasets where latency is not a constraint. Batch is significantly cheaper per prediction.

questions.q: Your team needs a single managed Google Cloud platform that supports the entire ML lifecycle — labeling, training (both AutoML and custom), hyperparameter tuning, model registry, online and batch prediction, and pipeline orchestration. Which service should you standardize on?
choices: BigQuery ML — SQL-based model training on warehouse data
Dataproc — managed Hadoop and Spark clusters
Cloud Composer — managed Apache Airflow for workflow orchestration
Vertex AI — the unified, managed end-to-end ML platform
questions.explanation: Vertex AI is Google Cloud's unified, end-to-end managed ML platform. It consolidates AutoML, custom training, Feature Store, Pipelines, Model Registry, Endpoints (online + batch), Explainable AI, Vizier hyperparameter tuning and Model Monitoring in one place. BigQuery ML is for SQL-based modeling inside BigQuery only, Dataproc is for Hadoop/Spark analytics, and Cloud Composer is a generic Airflow orchestrator — none of them is the unified ML platform.

questions.q: A data analyst with strong SQL skills but limited Python experience needs to train a regression model directly on a 2 TB BigQuery table without exporting the data. Which approach minimizes effort and data movement?
choices: Export the table to Cloud Storage as CSV, then train with Vertex AI custom container jobs
Spin up a Dataproc cluster and train with Spark MLlib reading via the BigQuery connector
Use BigQuery ML and run a CREATE MODEL statement that trains in place on BigQuery
Stream the rows through Pub/Sub and train an online model with Vertex AI Workbench
questions.explanation: BigQuery ML lets analysts train models with familiar CREATE MODEL SQL syntax, executing inside BigQuery so no data is moved. It supports linear/logistic regression, boosted trees, ARIMA Plus, k-means, matrix factorization and can import or export to Vertex AI. Exporting to GCS for Vertex AI custom training, running Spark MLlib on Dataproc, or streaming through Pub/Sub all require Python and add unnecessary infrastructure for this SQL-centric scenario.

questions.q: Two teams keep computing the same customer-recency and 30-day-purchase features from raw logs, leading to subtle differences between training and serving. You need a central, low-latency store that reuses identical feature definitions across both pipelines. Which Vertex AI capability fits best?
choices: Vertex AI Pipelines — DAG orchestration for ML workflows
Vertex AI Feature Store — managed registry and online/offline feature serving
Vertex AI Model Registry — versioned catalog of trained models
Vertex AI Workbench — managed JupyterLab notebooks
questions.explanation: Vertex AI Feature Store centralizes feature definitions and serves the same values to both training (offline, batch reads) and online prediction (low-latency lookups), eliminating training-serving skew caused by duplicated transformation code. Pipelines orchestrate workflows, the Model Registry catalogs trained models, and Workbench provides notebooks — none of them is a feature store.

questions.q: After deploying a fraud-detection model to a Vertex AI endpoint, you notice gradually degrading precision. The input feature distributions in production have shifted compared to the training data, but the ground-truth labels arrive weeks later. Which Model Monitoring signal should you configure to detect this issue early?
choices: Training-serving skew — compares production inputs to the training dataset
Feature attribution drift only — ranks SHAP attribution changes per request
Endpoint latency alerts in Cloud Monitoring — fires when p95 exceeds the SLO
Prediction drift — compares the live input distribution to a recent production baseline
questions.explanation: Vertex AI Model Monitoring distinguishes two distribution-shift signals. Training-serving skew compares serving inputs against the original training data and assumes the training distribution is still the ground truth. Prediction drift compares the current serving distribution against a recent serving baseline and is the right signal when the world is evolving over time and you want to catch gradual change. Feature attribution drift is complementary but not the primary input-distribution detector, and latency alerts say nothing about data quality.

questions.q: A regulated insurer must reproduce, on demand, the exact data, code and hyperparameters used to train any production model — and run that training the same way each month with versioned artifacts. Which Vertex AI service should orchestrate the end-to-end workflow?
choices: Cloud Functions triggered from Cloud Storage object-finalize events
Vertex AI Pipelines — managed Kubeflow Pipelines with metadata lineage tracking
Cloud Run jobs invoked from a Cloud Scheduler cron entry
BigQuery scheduled queries chained through saved query history
questions.explanation: Vertex AI Pipelines runs Kubeflow Pipelines (or TFX) workflows on a managed, serverless backend and automatically records every artifact, parameter and execution in Vertex ML Metadata — giving the lineage and reproducibility regulators require. Cloud Functions and Cloud Run jobs can run code on a trigger but do not provide ML-aware artifact tracking; BigQuery scheduled queries are SQL-only and do not orchestrate training, evaluation and deployment as a typed DAG.

questions.q: A retail recommender must respond to web requests with personalized suggestions in under 200 ms. A separate weekly job needs to score 80 million users with the same model and write the results to BigQuery. How should you deploy this model in Vertex AI?
choices: Deploy to a Vertex AI endpoint for online prediction; use the same model for batch prediction jobs against the BigQuery source
Deploy only an online endpoint and call it from a Dataflow pipeline once per user every week
Run a Vertex AI batch prediction job for every web request and cache the results in Memorystore
Export the model to TensorFlow.js and run all inference in the browser to bypass the endpoint
questions.explanation: Vertex AI distinguishes online prediction (a deployed endpoint backing a low-latency HTTP API, ideal for the 200 ms web path) from batch prediction (a job that reads a BigQuery or GCS input and writes predictions back without a deployed endpoint, ideal for the weekly 80 M-user score). One registered model in the Model Registry can back both — there is no need to invent per-request batch jobs, fan out an endpoint with Dataflow, or push the model into the browser.

questions.q: Your model approves or denies loan applications and must produce, per request, the contribution of each input feature to the score so adjudicators can justify decisions. Which Vertex AI feature provides per-prediction feature attributions for tabular models?
choices: Vertex AI Vizier — a black-box hyperparameter tuning service
Cloud DLP — detection and redaction of sensitive data
Vertex Explainable AI — sampled Shapley and Integrated Gradients attributions
Vertex AI Matching Engine — high-scale approximate nearest-neighbor search
questions.explanation: Vertex Explainable AI returns per-feature attributions for every prediction using methods such as sampled Shapley (tabular AutoML and custom models), Integrated Gradients and XRAI (deep models). It is the right primitive for justifying individual decisions. Vizier tunes hyperparameters, DLP redacts sensitive data, and Matching Engine is a vector search service — none of them produces per-prediction attributions.

questions.q: You must train a deep image classifier on 100 GB of labeled photos as fast as possible, with as little code change as possible from your existing single-GPU TensorFlow script. Which distributed-training strategy should you use on Vertex AI custom training?
choices: tf.distribute.MirroredStrategy on one multi-GPU machine — synchronous data parallelism across local GPUs
tf.distribute.ParameterServerStrategy across 20 CPU workers — asynchronous parameter updates
A custom Python loop that shards data across Cloud Functions invocations
tf.distribute.experimental.CentralStorageStrategy across regional Cloud Storage buckets
questions.explanation: For a single, dense deep-learning model that fits in GPU memory, MirroredStrategy on a single multi-GPU machine gives synchronous all-reduce data parallelism with essentially no code change — wrap model creation in `strategy.scope()` and Keras handles the rest. ParameterServerStrategy targets very large sparse models or huge clusters and adds async-update complexity, Cloud Functions are not built for long GPU training jobs, and CentralStorageStrategy across regional buckets is not a real distribution strategy.

nodes.title: GCP Dataflow (Professional Data Engineer): Key Ideas
nodes.content: Cloud Dataflow is GCP's fully managed stream and batch processing service built on Apache Beam. The PDE exam tests Beam programming model concepts — pipelines, PCollections, transforms, windows, watermarks — and when to use Dataflow vs Dataproc vs BigQuery.

flashcards.front: What is a PCollection and a PTransform in Apache Beam?
flashcards.back: PCollection (Parallel Collection): an immutable, distributed dataset that flows through a Beam pipeline — can be bounded (batch) or unbounded (stream). PTransform: an operation applied to a PCollection to produce another PCollection — examples are `ParDo` (element-wise processing), `GroupByKey`, `Combine`, `Flatten`, and `Partition`. Pipelines are DAGs of PTransforms connected by PCollections.

flashcards.front: Fixed windows vs sliding windows vs session windows — when do you use each?
flashcards.back: Fixed (tumbling) windows: non-overlapping, equal-sized time buckets — 'events from 10:00–10:05'. Sliding windows: overlapping, defined by size + slide interval — 'last 5-min average, updated every 1 min'. Session windows: activity-based, closed after a gap of inactivity — 'group events from a user session separated by > 30 s of idle'. Fixed for simple aggregations, session for user behavior.

flashcards.front: What is a watermark and why does late data matter?
flashcards.back: A watermark is Beam's estimate of how far event time has progressed — it tells the system 'we probably have all events up to T'. When the watermark passes a window's end, the window is emitted. Late data (events that arrive after the watermark) can be handled by triggers and `allowed_lateness` — you can re-fire a window when late data arrives. Ignoring late data produces incorrect aggregations in streaming pipelines.

flashcards.front: Side inputs in Dataflow — what are they for?
flashcards.back: A side input is extra data made available to a `ParDo` transform beyond the main PCollection. Used when you need to look up a value for every element — e.g., a small dimension table loaded as a side input so each event can be enriched without a join. Side inputs are broadcast to all worker shards; keep them small (< 100 MB) or performance degrades.

questions.q: You are tuning seven hyperparameters of a custom model and want Google to use Bayesian optimization to converge on strong settings with fewer training trials than a manual grid search. Which Vertex AI capability should you call?
choices: Vertex AI Vizier — black-box optimization service exposed via hyperparameter tuning jobs
Vertex AI Feature Store — online and offline feature serving
Vertex AI TensorBoard — visualization of training metrics
Vertex AI Model Registry — versioned catalog of trained models
questions.explanation: Vertex AI Vizier is Google's black-box optimization service; in Vertex AI it powers hyperparameter tuning jobs that use Bayesian (and other) search algorithms to find good hyperparameters in far fewer trials than grid or random search. Feature Store serves features, TensorBoard visualizes metrics, and the Model Registry catalogs models — none of them performs hyperparameter optimization.

questions.q: You have 8 TB of raw JSON logs that you want to convert into a sharded, compressed format that TensorFlow input pipelines can stream efficiently and shuffle across workers. Which combination minimizes preprocessing latency at training time?
choices: Keep the JSON files in Cloud Storage and read them line-by-line with tf.data.TextLineDataset
Load every record into a Cloud SQL table and read with the SQLAlchemy adapter
Preprocess with Dataflow and write sharded TFRecord files to Cloud Storage; consume with tf.data.TFRecordDataset and interleave()
Import the data into BigQuery and use the legacy SQL EXPORT statement during each epoch
questions.explanation: The Google-recommended pattern for large TensorFlow training jobs is to preprocess once with Dataflow into sharded TFRecord files on Cloud Storage, then stream them at training time with `tf.data.TFRecordDataset` plus `interleave` and `prefetch`. TFRecords are a compact, protobuf-based, easily-shardable format optimized for sequential reads. JSON line scans, Cloud SQL fan-out and per-epoch BigQuery exports all add latency and cost per training step.

questions.q: A model that scores resumes is found to under-rank candidates from one demographic group. Before retraining, you want to measure whether the model satisfies a fairness criterion such as equal opportunity across protected groups. Which approach is most appropriate within Google Cloud's responsible-AI tooling?
choices: Drop the protected attribute from the training set and assume the model is now fair
Use Vertex Explainable AI together with a fairness analysis (e.g., the What-If Tool or sliced evaluation) to compare per-group metrics such as true-positive rates
Increase the learning rate so the model converges to a more uniform output distribution
Switch from AutoML to a custom model — custom models are inherently fair
questions.explanation: Responsible-AI practice on Google Cloud is to evaluate slices of the data per protected group and compare metrics (true-positive rate, false-positive rate, calibration). Vertex Explainable AI and the What-If Tool support this kind of sliced/fairness analysis, and Vertex AI Model Evaluation reports per-slice metrics. Simply dropping the protected attribute does not remove bias (proxy features remain), tweaking the learning rate has no relationship to fairness, and AutoML vs. custom is unrelated to whether a model is fair.

questions.q: A data-science team prefers JupyterLab and wants a fully managed development environment on Google Cloud with pre-installed TensorFlow and PyTorch, access to GPUs, and built-in connectors to BigQuery and Cloud Storage — without managing the underlying VM lifecycle themselves. Which service should they use?
choices: App Engine flexible environment with a custom Jupyter Docker image
Compute Engine VM with a manually installed Anaconda distribution
Cloud Run serving a stateless Jupyter container behind an HTTPS endpoint
Vertex AI Workbench — managed JupyterLab notebooks integrated with Vertex AI services
questions.explanation: Vertex AI Workbench provides fully managed (and user-managed) JupyterLab instances with pre-built TensorFlow, PyTorch and CUDA images, optional GPUs, idle shutdown, and one-click BigQuery and Cloud Storage browsers. It is the recommended notebook environment for Vertex AI. App Engine Flex and Cloud Run are stateless application platforms not designed as interactive notebooks, and a raw Compute Engine VM puts OS, drivers and lifecycle back on the team.

questions.q: Ten million customer records in Cloud Storage must be scored once per night by a trained Vertex AI model; no real-time access is needed and cost should be minimal. Which serving approach fits?
choices: A Vertex AI batch prediction job reading from Cloud Storage and writing results back
A dedicated online endpoint scaled up nightly by a cron job and scaled down afterwards
Streaming the records through Pub/Sub into an always-on prediction pipeline
Embedding the model in a Cloud Run service invoked record-by-record from a scheduler
questions.explanation: Batch prediction is purpose-built for offline scoring: it provisions workers for the job's duration, reads input from Cloud Storage/BigQuery, writes predictions out, then releases all resources. Endpoints (managed or Cloud Run) keep serving infrastructure alive and pay per-record invocation overhead; streaming infrastructure is for continuous arrival, not a nightly bulk job.

questions.q: A new fraud-model version must receive 5% of production requests while the current version keeps 95%, with instant rollback if metrics degrade. How is this done on Vertex AI?
choices: Create a second endpoint for the new model and update client DNS weights gradually
Deploy both model versions to the same endpoint and configure the traffic split 95/5
Use a Cloud Load Balancer with header-based routing in front of two prediction services
Export both models to BigQuery ML and alternate which one scheduled queries invoke
questions.explanation: Vertex AI endpoints support multiple deployed models with percentage traffic splitting — set 95/5, watch metrics, then shift to 100/0 or roll back by editing the split, no client changes. Separate endpoints with DNS weighting put rollout logic in the client; a custom LB duplicates a built-in feature; BQML export isn't an online-serving canary mechanism.

questions.q: A team retrains weekly: data validation → preprocessing → training → evaluation → conditional deployment. Steps must be orchestrated, parameterized, and every artifact tracked with lineage. What should they build?
choices: A chain of Cloud Functions triggered by Pub/Sub messages, each function passing intermediate file paths to the next step in the message payload
A cron-driven Compute Engine VM running a monolithic Python script for the whole sequence
A Vertex AI Pipeline (Kubeflow Pipelines SDK) with each step as a component, run on a schedule
A BigQuery scheduled query that calls remote model training functions in sequence
questions.explanation: Vertex AI Pipelines executes KFP component DAGs serverlessly, with parameters, caching, conditional branches (deploy only if evaluation passes) and automatic artifact lineage in ML Metadata. Function chains and cron scripts give orchestration without lineage, retries or visualization; BigQuery scheduled queries are not a training orchestrator.

questions.q: A product team with no ML engineers needs an image classifier for 12 product categories from 40,000 labeled photos, prioritizing time-to-market over squeezing out the last point of accuracy. What does Google recommend?
choices: Train a custom TensorFlow CNN with Vertex AI custom training and a tuned ResNet backbone
AutoML image classification on Vertex AI, training from the labeled dataset directly
Run BigQuery ML with a logistic regression model over embeddings computed in SQL
Hand-label rules in a decision tree exported from a spreadsheet of image attributes
questions.explanation: AutoML handles architecture search, training and tuning from labeled data with no model code — the fast path when the team lacks ML expertise and the problem is a standard modality. Custom training buys flexibility the team can't exploit; BQML doesn't natively train on images; rule-based classification doesn't work on pixels.

nodes.title: Part 3: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Part 3. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: Training a large model costs too much on on-demand GPUs. Runs last ~20 hours and can resume from checkpoints. Which cost optimization does Google recommend FIRST?
flashcards.back: Spot capacity is 60-90% cheaper, and checkpoint-resume makes preemption tolerable for long fault-tolerant training — the canonical first lever. A 3-year TPU reservation is a capacity commitment, not a quick saving; cutting data sacrifices model quality for cost; CPUs cost less per hour but far more per training run for deep learning.

flashcards.front: For which workload profile would a TPU generally be preferred over GPUs on Google Cloud?
flashcards.back: TPUs excel at large-scale dense linear algebra under XLA compilation (JAX, TensorFlow, PyTorch/XLA) — big transformers with large batches are the textbook case. Tree models and branching code don't map to systolic arrays; double-precision irregular workloads favor CPUs/HPC GPUs; custom C++ ops break the XLA path TPUs require.

flashcards.front: A model performs well offline but poorly in production. Investigation shows the serving path computes the 'days_since_last_purchase' feature with different logic than the training pipeline did. What is this failure called, and what is the standard prevention?
flashcards.back: When training and serving compute features differently, offline metrics stop predicting online behavior — training-serving skew. The fix is a single source of feature logic: a feature store (e.g. Vertex AI Feature Store) or one shared transformation library invoked by both paths. Drift is the world changing over time; leakage and underfitting are different pathologies.

flashcards.front: A semantic product-search feature must find the most similar items to a query embedding among 200 million item embeddings with millisecond latency. Which Google Cloud service is built for this?
flashcards.back: Vertex AI Vector Search (formerly Matching Engine) serves approximate-nearest-neighbor queries over billions of vectors at millisecond latency using ScaNN-style indexes. Brute-force ORDER BY in BigQuery is a batch scan, B-trees cannot index high-dimensional similarity, and an in-RAM linear scan of 200M vectors per query is neither fast nor economical.

questions.q: Training a large model costs too much on on-demand GPUs. Runs last ~20 hours and can resume from checkpoints. Which cost optimization does Google recommend FIRST?
choices: Move the workload to a single TPU v5 pod slice reserved for three years upfront through a committed-use discount agreement
Use Spot (preemptible) VMs/GPUs for training, with regular checkpointing so preempted jobs resume
Reduce the training dataset by 80% so each run completes within the free tier
Switch all training to CPUs, which have lower hourly prices than accelerators
questions.explanation: Spot capacity is 60-90% cheaper, and checkpoint-resume makes preemption tolerable for long fault-tolerant training — the canonical first lever. A 3-year TPU reservation is a capacity commitment, not a quick saving; cutting data sacrifices model quality for cost; CPUs cost less per hour but far more per training run for deep learning.

questions.q: For which workload profile would a TPU generally be preferred over GPUs on Google Cloud?
choices: A scikit-learn gradient-boosted-trees model trained on tabular data with heavy branching
A simulation engine dominated by double-precision physics computations and highly irregular memory access patterns across very large sparse meshes
Serving a small model where each request requires custom C++ pre-processing operators
Training a large transformer with big batch sizes, dominated by dense matrix multiplication, in an XLA-compatible framework
questions.explanation: TPUs excel at large-scale dense linear algebra under XLA compilation (JAX, TensorFlow, PyTorch/XLA) — big transformers with large batches are the textbook case. Tree models and branching code don't map to systolic arrays; double-precision irregular workloads favor CPUs/HPC GPUs; custom C++ ops break the XLA path TPUs require.

questions.q: A model performs well offline but poorly in production. Investigation shows the serving path computes the 'days_since_last_purchase' feature with different logic than the training pipeline did. What is this failure called, and what is the standard prevention?
choices: Training-serving skew; prevent it by sharing one feature computation (feature store or shared transform code) between training and serving
Concept drift; prevent it by retraining the model on a more frequent fixed schedule so production data never diverges too far from the training distribution
Label leakage; prevent it by removing the feature from the training dataset entirely
Underfitting; prevent it by increasing model capacity and training for more epochs
questions.explanation: When training and serving compute features differently, offline metrics stop predicting online behavior — training-serving skew. The fix is a single source of feature logic: a feature store (e.g. Vertex AI Feature Store) or one shared transformation library invoked by both paths. Drift is the world changing over time; leakage and underfitting are different pathologies.

questions.q: A semantic product-search feature must find the most similar items to a query embedding among 200 million item embeddings with millisecond latency. Which Google Cloud service is built for this?
choices: BigQuery with an ORDER BY cosine-distance clause over the full embeddings table
Cloud SQL with a B-tree index over the embedding vectors stored as JSON arrays
Vertex AI Vector Search (approximate nearest neighbor at scale)
Memorystore Redis storing all embeddings in RAM and scanning them per query
questions.explanation: Vertex AI Vector Search (formerly Matching Engine) serves approximate-nearest-neighbor queries over billions of vectors at millisecond latency using ScaNN-style indexes. Brute-force ORDER BY in BigQuery is a batch scan, B-trees cannot index high-dimensional similarity, and an in-RAM linear scan of 200M vectors per query is neither fast nor economical.

questions.q: Model monitoring on a Vertex AI endpoint raises a feature-drift alert. The MLOps team wants this signal to automatically kick off the validated retraining pipeline. What is the recommended wiring?
choices: Grant the monitoring job IAM permission to redeploy the model directly to the endpoint
Route the alert notification (Pub/Sub) to a trigger — e.g. a Cloud Function — that submits the Vertex AI Pipeline run
Configure the endpoint to fall back automatically to the previous model version whenever the drift metric exceeds its configured alerting threshold
Lower the drift threshold until alerts stop appearing in the monitoring dashboard
questions.explanation: The continuous-training pattern: monitoring alerts publish to a channel (Pub/Sub/alerting), a lightweight trigger consumes the event and launches the pipeline, which retrains, evaluates and only then deploys. Monitoring jobs shouldn't deploy models (no evaluation gate); rolling back to an older model worsens drift; silencing alerts ignores the problem.

questions.q: A team has 500,000 unlabeled product photos and needs bounding-box labels for object detection. Internal staff cannot absorb the work. What does Vertex AI offer for this?
choices: A data labeling job, defining instructions and label sets for human labelers to annotate the dataset
AutoML pre-labeling, which first trains the object detector on the raw photos and then infers all bounding-box labels itself without any human involvement
BigQuery's ML.ANNOTATE function applying vision labels through a SQL interface
Dataplex data profiling, which extracts bounding boxes during metadata scanning
questions.explanation: Vertex AI data labeling jobs send datasets to human annotators with your instructions, label taxonomy and quality controls — the path when ground truth doesn't exist and staff can't produce it. You cannot train a detector without labels (so 'pre-labeling' is circular as the primary source); the BigQuery and Dataplex options describe capabilities that don't perform bounding-box annotation.
